text: Quantum SDKs break more often, and more silently, than most classical dependencies. A circuit that computed one answer under an older Qiskit version can compute a numerically different answer under a newer one without raising a single error. Dependency management here isn't a formality — it's how you prevent that.

This lesson covers why quantum SDKs churn faster than typical classical libraries, the difference between a breaking change that errors loudly and one that silently changes numerical output, how to pin exact versions with a lockfile, and how to isolate incompatible SDKs like Qiskit and a Q-sharp toolchain using separate environments.

There are two categories of SDK change, and the second is far more dangerous. A loud break removes the old API entirely, so your code raises an error immediately — annoying, but safe, because you find out the moment you run anything. A silent break is when the API still exists and still runs, but its numerical behavior changed, for example a transpiler's default optimization behavior shifting between versions. Silent breaks don't trigger an error for you to notice — your test suite running against a pinned, known-good environment is what actually catches them.

For most Python projects, a loose version range is reasonable because minor updates are safe. For quantum SDKs, prefer exact pins in pyproject.toml, and generate and commit a full lockfile alongside it. Without a committed lockfile, two developers installing the exact same pinned version on the same day can still end up with different transitive dependency versions underneath it, which can change transpiler behavior without anyone touching a single line of their own code.

A project that needs both Qiskit and Microsoft's Q-sharp or QDK toolchain shouldn't install both into one environment — Q-sharp runs on its own .NET-based interop layer with its own release cadence, and the two ecosystems aren't designed to coexist cleanly. The practical fix is separate environments per SDK, invoked as subprocesses or through a thin API boundary, which Chapter 3 builds into a full architectural pattern.

Before bumping a pinned SDK version, follow a short checklist: read the SDK's changelog for every version in the range you're crossing, not just the latest notes; run the full test suite from Chapter 2 against the new version on an isolated branch, where a loud break fails immediately; and re-run your statistical tests, comparing against previously recorded, pinned-environment results, which is what actually catches a silent break in numerical behavior.
Next lesson turns to documentation — specifically, what a quantum function's docstring needs to say that a classical docstring usually doesn't.
